questions.enonce_markdown:
How important was the call of Samuel in the life of the Israelites?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Samuel was born to Hannah, who had vowed to dedicate her child to the Lord (1 Samuel 1), and was brought up in the sanctuary at Shiloh under the priest Eli. His call, reported in 1 Samuel 3, came at a time of religious and moral decline: "the word of the Lord was rare in those days; visions were not widespread" (1 Samuel 3:1). Its importance for Israel can be seen in several areas.

**1. It ended a period of silence and decay.** The priesthood of Eli was corrupt: his sons Hophni and Phinehas abused their office (1 Samuel 2). In his first message God announced judgement on Eli's house for failing to restrain them (1 Samuel 3:11-14). The call therefore signalled the end of the old leadership and a fresh start.

**2. It restored prophecy and divine guidance.** After the call, "the Lord was with Samuel and let none of his words fall to the ground", and "all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was a trustworthy prophet of the Lord" (1 Samuel 3:19-20). Israel again had a recognised spokesman of God.

**3. It produced a national leader with several roles.** Samuel acted as prophet, judge and intercessor, and in some passages as priest offering sacrifice. At Mizpah he led the people to repent and to put away foreign gods, and God gave victory over the Philistines at Ebenezer (1 Samuel 7). He judged Israel on a yearly circuit (Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpah) and from Ramah.

**4. It prepared the transition from the judges to the monarchy.** When the elders demanded a king (1 Samuel 8), Samuel prayed, warned them of the cost of kingship and, under God's direction, anointed Saul (1 Samuel 9-10). Later he anointed David (1 Samuel 16). He thus linked the age of the judges to the royal dynasty from which later Israel's hopes would come.

**5. It restated the principles of the covenant.** Samuel taught that obedience matters more than ritual ("to obey is better than sacrifice", 1 Samuel 15:22), and in his farewell speech (1 Samuel 12) he called both people and king to remain faithful to the Lord.

**6. It established the prophetic office.** Samuel is often seen as the first of the great prophets who would later correct kings.

**Conclusion.** The call of Samuel was a turning point: it replaced a failing priesthood with a prophetic leadership, renewed the people's faith, and opened the way for the monarchy and for David. It was therefore of great importance in Israelite life.
